source: Woods & Cook (c.1999) Perspectives on Human Error: Hindsight Biases and Local Rationality
finding: Defines fixation as failure to revise a situation assessment despite opportunities to revise. Needs persistence over time plus cues that were available. The first assessment is usually reasonable.
numbers: Criteria: (1) persistence, (2) revision cues available. Cites De Keyser & Woods 1990, Johnson 1981/1988, Gaba & DeAnda 1989; Three Mile Island as case. No effect sizes.
quote: fail to revise their situation assessment or course of action and maintain an inappropriate judgment
limits: Narrative review; case based; hindsight makes the fix look obvious. Publication year not shown in the text; c.1999 from the handbook chapter.
agent_relevance: Gives a code-checkable definition of an impasse: same hypothesis kept for N steps while new evidence contradicts it. Our detector should test both criteria, not just repetition.

source: Woods & Cook (c.1999) garden path problems
finding: Garden-path problems: early cues point to a plausible wrong answer and later, weaker cues point to the right one. Fixation here is not lack of knowledge but a normally good process applied to a bad class of problem.
numbers: Quoted from Johnson, Moen & Thompson 1988. No numbers in this chapter.
quote: early cues strongly suggest [plausible but] incorrect answers, and later, usually weaker cues suggest answers that are correct
limits: Task-genotype argument, not a measured rate. Boundary: fixation is defined against problems with that cue order.
agent_relevance: Order of evidence matters. The scaffold should re-weigh late weak contradicting evidence against the early strong hypothesis, and tag items where early cues were misleading.

source: Woods & Cook (c.1999) trade-off between revising and coherence (thematic vagabonding)
finding: Two opposite failures: attention that never shifts gives fixation; attention that shifts on every signal gives thematic vagabonding (Dorner 1983). Revision has a cost.
numbers: No numbers. Dorner 1983 cited for vagabonding.
limits: Conceptual. No test of where the best switching rate lies.
agent_relevance: Supports G1: doubt only on a signal. Forced doubt on a schedule is the vagabonding failure, in line with our word-puzzle drop 92% to 75%.

source: Woods & Cook (c.1999) remedies for fixation: fresh viewpoint, devil's advocate, better feedback display
finding: Data on successful revision show it usually takes a person with a fresh point of view to break a fixation. Three design routes: fresh-view architecture, a critic role, better process feedback.
numbers: Source claim from Woods et al. 1987 (nuclear power, post-TMI). No effect size reported in the chapter.
limits: Based on incident reviews, not controlled trials. Devil's advocate cites Schwenk & Cosier 1980.
agent_relevance: A second pass with a clean context (no earlier reasoning) is the closest analogue. Matches G4 caution: it must be a fresh context, not a persona of the same samples.

source: Howard, Gaba et al. (1992) Anesthesiologists' management of simulated critical incidents (Anesthesiology)
finding: Simulator study of 30 anesthesiologists. Fixation errors, failure to revise a plan with inconsistent cues, occurred in 63% of subjects. Experience did not prevent serious errors.
numbers: N=30 (10 residents, 10 faculty, 10 private practice). 63% fixation errors. 40% diagnosed simulated anaphylaxis; 27% adequately treated myocardial ischemia; 30% managed cardiac arrest per ACLS. All experienced staff diagnosed esophageal intubation; 2 residents did not. More information gathering in anaphylaxis went with correct diagnosis and fewer treatment errors. Time since last ACLS training predicted arrest management.
limits: Abstract read via Europe PMC (truncated at 250 words); no per-group breakdown of the 63%. Early PC simulator; small N; no control arm. Author list not confirmed from the page.
agent_relevance: Fixation is common (about 6 in 10) even for experts, so an impasse detector cannot assume it is rare. Information gathering predicted success, which supports a check that counts new evidence sought after a first hypothesis.

source: DeAnda & Gaba (1990) Unplanned incidents during comprehensive anesthesia simulation (Anesth Analg 71:77-82)
finding: In 19 simulations with first- and second-year residents, unplanned incidents were mostly human error; fixation errors were about one fifth.
numbers: Search snippet only: human errors 65.9%, equipment failures 3%, fixation errors 20.5%, unknown causes 10.6%.
limits: Not opened beyond a search snippet; details unverified. Bucket definitions may differ from Howard 1992.
agent_relevance: Gives a second rate for fixation (about 20% of unplanned incidents) at the novice end, to compare with 63% in Howard 1992. Verify before citing.

source: Parasuraman & Manzey (2010) Complacency and bias in human use of automation: an attentional integration (Hum Factors)
finding: Review of empirical studies. Complacency appears under multi-task load and in naive and expert participants. Automation bias gives both omission and commission errors, is found in experts, and is not prevented by training or instructions.
numbers: No pooled effect size in the abstract. Stated: not overcome by simple practice; not prevented by training or instructions.
limits: Abstract read only. Review, not a formal meta-analysis. Mostly aviation and lab tasks.
agent_relevance: A model that follows an automated hint (a tool output, a prior step) will under-check it. Instructions alone will not fix it; add code checks on tool output.

source: Goddard, Roudsari & Wyatt (2012) Automation bias: a systematic review of frequency, effect mediators, and mitigators (JAMIA)
finding: Systematic review. 74 of 13,821 papers met criteria. Workload, task complexity and time pressure raised automation bias; training, user accountability, advice placement, confidence display and showing information rather than a recommendation reduced it.
numbers: 13,821 retrieved, 74 included. Mediators: cognitive style, experience, trust, confidence, workload, complexity, time constraint. Mitigators as listed.
limits: Abstract read only. Healthcare focus. Heterogeneous designs; no pooled effect.
agent_relevance: Time pressure and complexity worsen over-reliance. Giving the agent evidence rather than a recommended answer matches G5 (no proposed answer shown to the judge).

source: Lyell & Coiera (2017) Automation bias and verification complexity: a systematic review (JAMIA)
finding: Contrary to the view that automation bias needs multitasking, it was found in single tasks, mostly diagnosis with high verification complexity. Authors link it to cognitive load.
numbers: 890 papers screened, 40 included (6 in health care). Few studies reported significance against a control.
limits: Abstract read only. Fragmented literature; inconsistent reporting.
agent_relevance: Hard-to-verify steps invite acceptance. Make verification cheap and code-based so the agent is not asked to judge things it cannot check.

source: Chen et al. (2025, MLSys) AIOpsLab: framework to evaluate AI agents for autonomous clouds
finding: 48-problem microservice fault benchmark over detection, localization, root cause analysis and mitigation. LLM agents beat classic AIOps tools on detection and localization but do poorly on RCA and mitigation.
numbers: Overall: best FLASH 59.32%, worst GPT-3.5-w-shell 15.25% (confirmed in text; other two overall figures, 49.15% and 55.93%, belong to GPT-4-w-shell and ReAct but the extract is scrambled). Detection: FLASH 100%, ReAct 76.92%, GPT-4 69.23%. RCA: ReAct 45.45%, GPT-4 40.90%, FLASH 36.36%. Mitigation: FLASH 54.55%, GPT-4 27.27%, GPT-3.5 0%.
limits: Small problem set (about 13 per cell for detection and localization, 11 for RCA and mitigation). PDF table text scrambled; some per-agent cells uncertain. Older models (GPT-3.5/4).
agent_relevance: Measured gap from detect to fix. Mitigation, which needs a changed plan after a failed action, is where agents break. Fits a revise-from-real-output rule (G2).

source: Chen et al. (2025) AIOpsLab: step limit and repeated actions
finding: More steps help only some agents. GPT-3.5 plateaus after 5 steps. Agents repeat the same malformed API call, up to 14 times in a 20-step case. Round-robin multi-agent chatter wastes steps.
numbers: FLASH reaches 59.32% at step limit 20; GPT-3.5 gains nothing past 5 steps. Repeated identical error: up to 14 times in 20 steps (GPT-3.5-w-shell). ReAct usually recovers from bad commands by reasoning.
quote: self-repair with environment feedback can saturate quickly for AIOps problems
limits: Observational failure analysis by the authors; no count of how many runs show repetition.
agent_relevance: Direct match to Woods's stuck-in-outdated-behaviour and cross-purposes patterns. A code counter on identical consecutive actions or errors is a cheap, valid impasse detector.

source: Chen et al. (2025) AIOpsLab: data overload
finding: Failed cases leaned more on raw metrics and trace calls; agents dumped raw telemetry into context, causing distraction and token exhaustion.
numbers: Action distribution in Figure 7 differs between success and failure; exact percentages not legible in the text extract.
limits: Correlational. Figure values not recovered.
agent_relevance: Raw data dumps are a sign of an agent without a hypothesis. Code should summarise tool output before the model sees it.

source: Jha et al. (2025) ITBench: evaluating AI agents across real-world IT automation tasks
finding: 94 real-world style IT scenarios. Agents resolved 13.8% of SRE scenarios, 25.2% of CISO scenarios, 0% of FinOps. Hard SRE scenarios were never mitigated.
numbers: SRE: 42 scenarios, 10 runs each. Best model GPT-4o: diagnosis pass@1 13.81%, mitigation 11.43%. By difficulty (GPT-4o): diagnosis Easy 36%, Medium 7.73%, Hard 5.0%; mitigation Easy 21%, Medium 12.27%, Hard 0.0%. Without trace data GPT-4o diagnosis fell 13.81% to 9.52% and mitigation to 2.86%.
limits: Open models weaker; GPT-4o is a 2024 model. Outcome varies between runs of the same scenario (non-determinism reported).
agent_relevance: Real dynamic-fault tasks are still mostly unsolved by LLM agents, with steep falloff by difficulty. Plan for failure and escalation; do not assume anomaly-response skill.

source: Roy et al. (2024) Exploring LLM-based agents for root cause analysis
finding: ReAct agent with retrieval tools reached about the same correctness as retrieval and chain-of-thought baselines on incident root cause, but hallucinated much less.
numbers: Correctness 35% (ReAct S+Q BM25) vs 39% (CoT and retrieval baseline k=10). Hallucination: 4% ReAct vs 12% baselines. 28 of 97 examples solved by all three. Among incorrect answers, 'Other' cause: 12% ReAct vs 32% retrieval and 45% CoT.
limits: Single company, 97 cases, offline reports with no live system. Lexical metrics within margin of error.
agent_relevance: Tool-using investigation lowers made-up causes but did not raise accuracy. Grounding cuts hallucination; it does not cure wrong hypotheses.

source: Huang et al. (2024, ICLR) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Without external feedback, asking a model to review and revise its answer does not help and often hurts. With oracle labels it helps a lot, so earlier gains came from the label.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 (round 1). GSM8K GPT-3.5 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7; GPT-4 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0. HotpotQA GPT-4 49.0 to 49.0 to 43.0. Oracle labels: GSM8K GPT-3.5 75.9 to 95.5, HotpotQA GPT-3.5 26.0 to 49.0. GPT-3.5 kept its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time.
limits: Prompts from earlier papers; 100 HotpotQA items; reasoning tasks only. Table text partly scrambled in extraction.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G1 and G2. A model should not revise on its own say-so; revise when code shows a failing output.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024, TACL) When can LLMs actually correct their own mistakes? A critical survey
finding: Survey finds: no prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs outside tasks exceptionally suited to it; self-correction works with reliable external feedback; large-scale fine-tuning enables it.
numbers: Three conclusions as stated in the abstract. Many studies used oracle information or weak initial prompts.
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs
limits: Survey of published studies; publication bias possible.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as Woods's fresh-viewpoint finding: break fixation with outside information (tool output, held-out checks), not more reflection by the same model.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Models find the first mistake in a chain-of-thought trace poorly, but fix it well when told where it is. Backtracking from the true location gains more than from a random one.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake: GPT-4 overall mistake-finding accuracy 52.87% with direct step prompting (best model); 5 tasks. Backtracking with true location: gains of +18 to +44 points on originally incorrect answers (multistep arithmetic +43.92, Dyck +18.04), losses of 0 to -11 on originally correct ones; random-location gains much smaller.
limits: Synthetic CoT traces from PaLM 2 at temperature 0; five algorithmic tasks; 2023-era models.
agent_relevance: Finding the error is the weak step, fixing is the strong one. Let code locate the fault (tests, diffs), then ask the model to repair that step. Matches G2.

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs get lost in multi-turn conversation
finding: 15 models drop on average 39% from single-turn to multi-turn with gradually revealed information. Most of the loss is unreliability, not aptitude. Models make early assumptions, propose answers too soon, then rely on those answers.
numbers: 200,000+ simulated conversations, 6 tasks, 15 LLMs, about $5,000 cost. Fig.1 headline about -35% average, aptitude loss about 15%, unreliability up 112%. Reasoning models o3 and DeepSeek-R1 included and also degrade.
quote: when LLMs take a wrong turn in a conversation, they get lost and do not recover
limits: Simulated user, generation tasks; not a fault-management setting. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM analogue to fixation: early commitment then failure to revise. Extra thinking budget did not remove it.

source: Laban et al. (2025) lost in conversation: interventions (recap, snowball, temperature)
finding: Repeating all earlier information each turn (snowball) recovers only 15-20% of the lost performance. Lowering temperature fixes single-turn reliability but barely helps multi-turn.
numbers: Snowball mitigates the FULL-to-SHARDED deterioration by 15-20% (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini; 4 tasks). Recap (final turn) better but still below FULL. Temperature 1.0 to 0 cut FULL unreliability 50-80%; in sharded runs GPT-4o gained only 15-20% and GPT-4o-mini none.
limits: Two models for the recap test. Recap needs knowing the last turn, so it is unrealistic.
agent_relevance: Prompt-level restatement helps a little. A code-held record of facts and a restart from a clean summary (not the old transcript) is worth testing instead.

source: Zhu et al. (2025) Where LLM agents fail and how they can learn from failures
finding: Early errors cascade; the root-cause step matters more than surface fixes. A debugging framework that locates the critical error and feeds targeted feedback back improves task success.
numbers: AgentDebug: all-correct accuracy 24.3% vs 0.3% for strongest baseline (+24 points); step accuracy 45.0% vs 28.0% (+17); up to 26% relative gain in task success on ALFWorld, GAIA and WebShop. Taxonomy covers memory, reflection, planning, action, system.
limits: Authors' own benchmark and method; not independently replicated. An LLM does the locating.
agent_relevance: Fix the root-cause step, not every symptom. Supports G2 with a design where the located failing step drives revision.

source: Zhu et al. (2025) AgentDebug ablation: root cause focus
finding: Ablations say that focusing on root-cause errors, rather than every surface mistake, is the source of the gain.
numbers: Exact ablation numbers not extracted this session.
limits: Only the qualitative statement recorded.
agent_relevance: An impasse handler should name one cause and one repair, not a list.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why do multi-agent LLM systems fail? (MAST)
finding: Taxonomy of 14 failure modes in 3 categories from 1,642 annotated traces of 7 multi-agent frameworks. Failure rate on tested systems 41% to 86.7%. Step repetition and reasoning-action mismatch are common.
numbers: MAST-Data 1,642 traces; taxonomy built from 150 traces, kappa 0.88; LLM judge kappa 0.77. FM-1.3 step repetition 15.7%, FM-1.5 unaware of stop condition 12.4%, FM-2.6 reasoning-action mismatch 13.2%, FM-2.3 task derailment 7.4%, FM-2.5 ignored input 1.9%.
limits: Percentages are shares of failure labels in this dataset, not per-step rates. Frameworks differ; Claude 3.7 had more FC1/FC2 failures than GPT-4o in MetaGPT.
agent_relevance: Maps onto Woods's patterns: step repetition (stuck), conversation reset and ignored input (cross purposes). Each is detectable by code on the log.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) MAST: interventions and verification failures
finding: Better role prompts fix some design failures but not inter-agent misalignment. Verification failures stay high across models.
numbers: Role specification change alone: +9.4% success (ChatDev, GPT-4o). Both GPT-4o and Claude 3.7 Sonnet show many verification failures in MetaGPT.
limits: Intervention tested on one framework.
agent_relevance: Do not expect a teamwork prompt to fix cross purposes. A single agent with code control, as in our design, avoids the problem.

source: Patronus AI (2025) TRAIL: trace reasoning and agentic issue localization
finding: Finding errors in long agent traces is very hard. The best model got 11% joint accuracy on error category plus location.
numbers: Gemini-2.5-Pro joint 0.183 (GAIA split) and 0.050 (SWE-Bench split); o3 joint 0.092 on GAIA; several models hit context-length limits on the SWE split.
quote: best GEMINI-2.5-PRO model scoring a mere 11% on TRAIL
limits: Authors' annotation; trace length limits some models; taxonomy chosen by authors. Author names not confirmed from the page.
agent_relevance: A model watching its own long trajectory will not reliably spot where it went wrong. The impasse detector must be code on counts and states, not model self-review.

source: Lou & Sun (2024) Anchoring bias in large language models: an experimental study
finding: LLMs are pulled by a biased first hint. Chain-of-thought, thoughts of principles, ignoring anchor hints and reflection did not remove the bias; gathering hints from comprehensive angles did better.
numbers: No effect sizes recovered from the extract (qualitative summary from abstract).
limits: Small study by school students; one dataset; effect sizes not recovered. Treat as weak.
agent_relevance: Early information anchors the model; reflection prompts do not undo it. Supports presenting several independent views of the evidence before any hypothesis.

source: Arriaga et al. (2013) A simulation-based trial of surgical-crisis checklists (NEJM)
finding: Randomized simulation trial: crisis checklists improved adherence to critical steps in operating-room crises.
numbers: From memory, NOT verified this session: 17 teams, 106 simulated cases; failure to adhere 23% without vs 6% with checklist.
limits: Abstract not available through the tool; numbers unverified. Do not cite until checked.
agent_relevance: External cognitive aids work for human crisis response; a code-held checklist of required checks is the analogue.

source: Boer et al. (2020) Effect of cognitive aids on adherence to best practice in deteriorating surgical patients (JAMA Surg)
finding: Randomized simulation trial. Cognitive aids cut omitted critical management steps from 33% to 10%.
numbers: 25 teams x 3 scenarios with aids, 25 teams x 3 without (75 scenarios per arm). 33% to 10% omitted steps, 70% relative reduction, P<.001; multivariate OR 0.63. Usability median 8.7/10.
limits: Abstract read via Europe PMC; ward-patient deterioration, not intraoperative; simulation; Amsterdam teams only; measures omitted steps, not fixation. Author names not confirmed from the page.
agent_relevance: Forced external checklists beat memory under crisis. Supports code-run required checks before an answer is accepted.
